utterances.text: I called my brother, who got up. We talked. We telephoned to our neighbours to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn anything from the telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Well, the people themselves didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do next?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We went outside our house and were joined by our neighbours. We discussed the situation. And a neighbour of the two people who worked for us invited us over for coffee. She had made coffee. So we went and had the coffee and went back to our own house after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that whose home that you went to? Who was these people who worked for you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: It was Esad Dagovic, who worked as a waiter in our pizzeria, and then there was Safet Dagovic, his brother, who worked in my shop, my game shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they live in relation to your home?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Taking it from my house, they lived about 50-odd metres to the left, in the direction of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had coffee at their house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour. Half an hour to an hour. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left the Dagovic home, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We went back to our own house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we," that's you and your brother, Hasan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you observe anything when you got back to your house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: The shooting continued and the explosions that could be heard. You could hear detonations, shots. It was still dark, so that you couldn't see anything yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were your neighbours at that time? Did you see any of them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards, when it was daybreak. The neighbours from the surrounding houses and buildings had all somehow gathered there in that new part attached to my house, and it was situated between an apartment building and my house. We gathered there and discussed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they seem?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They were terrified; just as we were. They didn't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We went into the house, and my brother called up Mr. Pisarevic on the telephone. He asked what we should do, and Pisarevic said that he would tell him but that he just had to see what was going on himself, to check it out. And then he phoned later on and said that we would just hand in our weapons and that everything would be all right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you during the afternoon and evening of that same date?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: For the most part, at home, in my own house. When I say "for the most part," I mean that I was in the house and in this catering establishment that was under construction, and we were able to see the road from there and to see what was going on in the road from that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe anything during the afternoon or evening hours on that road?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed that in the distance, there were some tanks and that they were moving along the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many tanks?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: There were tanks, and the transporters, or whatever they're called, APC's, similar to tanks, about five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were they coming from? From what direction?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They were coming from the direction of the memorial centre, Brcko, Orasje, that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Later that evening, what did you and your brother do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We spent that whole evening at home, waiting to see whether they would come to collect our weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone come that evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Nobody came to our house, not that day and not that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next day. Let's go to 10.00 in the morning, April 18th. What happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: At 10.00 in the morning on the 18th of April, heavy shooting could be heard near our house. Prior to that, we had lowered the blinds in our family house. And there was a shattering that could be heard at the entrance door, and my brother and I unlocked the door, and the door burst open, and I received a severe blow to my head from a rifle. I fell down in the hallway which led towards the bathroom, and I was a little -- I was taken aback and not feeling fully conscious. People in masked uniforms rushed into the house. They had been -- their faces were painted with some sort of paint. And when they got me up, they transferred me into the living-room. I saw that they were holding my brother up against the wall with a knife to his neck. They were swearing and beating him, and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe the uniforms that these people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: The people were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say you were struck with a rifle, which part of the rifle were you struck in the head with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: He hit me with the rifle butt in my head, which means the back part of the rifle which is usually placed on the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your condition after being hit with the butt of the rifle?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: For a short time, I was sort of semi-conscious or semi-unconscious, and I was so afraid. But from the blows and kicks with the boot, I came to pretty quickly, because I was afraid they would kick me in the face and head, which unfortunately did happen during the time that I spent in the different camps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you bleeding?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. My shirt, the shirt I was in, was more red than it was white while it was on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers were in your home, as best that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Well, there were not less than six or seven, as far as I remember. Perhaps even as many as ten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you're sitting on the floor at some point in the living-room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was sitting on the floor in the living-room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a soldier has a knife to your brother's neck?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He put him up against a wall between the entrance to two rooms; that is to say, the bedroom and children's room. He was put up against a wall there, and he held the knife up to him, hitting him with his other hand, and the others helped him beat him, and they beat him too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As they were beating your brother, Hasan, did they say anything to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They asked for money, valuables, jewellery, gold. And they were beating me and swearing at me. They cursed my Muslim mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the other soldiers doing in the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: The others were simply ransacking drawers of the cupboards and cabinets and they were throwing the furniture outside. They were ransacking it, searching. They went into the other rooms too. And quite simply, they were looting and destroying the furniture in the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they looking for, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were these soldiers looking for as they were looking through the drawers and through the furniture?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They were looking for money, for valuables, for gold and jewellery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons in the house?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We had laid out our weapons on the floor, along with the licences we had for the weapons, so that they didn't even look at the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever learn the names of the soldiers that were in your house, any of them?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. After a few days in camp, on the premises of the Territorial Defence, or rather, in the Territorial Defence storage room, I found out that they were called Laki, Zec, Avram, Lugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen these individuals before in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: No, I had never seen them before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you learn where these people had come from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. People said they were special units who had arrived from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything about their accents or their dress or anything that they did that indicated that they were from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. They spoke in the Ekavian dialect, which in our area was not used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what area is that dialect or accent used?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: That dialect is used in Serbia. It's not the most frequent but the only dialect used in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go to Lugar. What did Lugar do in your house? Did he harm you or your brother?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He beat us, and he was the first person who hit me on the head with a rifle butt in our house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he beat you with any other instruments, either you or Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: He beat us with a police truncheon. He kicked us, and he was wearing boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were these people in your home, these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but they beat us and held us there for about 20 minutes. Then they called for a car. This was a Golf. They pushed us in. They had a pistol pointed at my neck and head. As the car was driving, he kept changing the position. So it was sometimes pointed at my neck, sometimes at my head. And the man who was sitting in front held an automatic pistol pointed at my brother's head. And so we arrived at the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the police station, what did you observe?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: In front of the police station, there was a large group of uniformed men. They were wearing JNA uniforms and also police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did they do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They stood in two lines, and we had to pass through. They beat us with their weapons, they kicked us, they used police truncheons to hit us until we reached the entrance to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, as you passed through that gauntlet, were they saying anything as they beat you and your brother, Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They cursed our balija mothers, and as they were hitting us, they simply cursed our mothers. We tried to run through as fast as we could, although we stumbled from the blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you finally got inside the police station, what was your condition and what was the condition, the physical condition, of your brother, Hasan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We were all battered, exhausted from the blows. We were in pain all over our bodies. My head was aching. I have a -- I had a big gash in my head which kept bleeding. Everything was bloodstained; my clothes, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go once you arrived at the police station? To a certain office, or where did they bring you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They put us in the reception office in the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were both you and your brother in the same office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were at first. But after that, they put me on one side and my brother on another. They separated us. They threw him onto a table which was covered with a thick glass plate which was broken. They took off his trousers and his shirt, and then they beat him with police truncheons as he was lying naked on that broken glass on the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they" did it, who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They were the men who had entered our house. Stevo Todorovic was there, policemen wearing police uniforms, and also men wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as your brother is being beaten on that table, where are you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I was in another room which was directly opposite this one. And through the open door, you could see across the corridor, which was about a metre, a metre and a half away, so you could see the table through the open doors. It was -- I was about four and a half metres away from the table where my brother was being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as your brother was being beaten and you're watching it, were they saying anything to him?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. They asked for our cars. They cursed his Muslim mother. He asked where he had hidden the cars. They asked where the money was. That was it mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After they finished beating your brother, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Then they took us upstairs in the police station building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they bring you upstairs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They pushed us into an office upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that office upstairs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We remained in that office until the evening. I think it was about 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in that office -- or when you went into the office at first, was there anyone else present?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They put a guard in that office. The guard was wearing a police uniform and had a rifle, and they told him to watch the two of us carefully until their return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any other prisoners brought into that office?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: [redacted] Simnica Ramadani, and later on Sulejman Tihic was also brought in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone enter the room during the time you were there, you and the others?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. A young lieutenant walked in who was wearing a JNA uniform, and he questioned us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else enter the room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Lugar came in after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did Lugar do?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Lugar beat my brother and me. He asked about our cars. We then gave him the keys of our jeep, which was in the garage next to the house. And for the moment, this satisfied him, but then he noticed the thick gold chains we were wearing around our necks, and he tried to pull them off. But we were afraid that he would hurt us even more, so my brother and I took off our gold chains and put them in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Lugar beat you in that office, did he use any implement or instrument?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He used a police truncheon. And since we were sitting on the floor, he would often kick us with his booted feet in the chest or wherever his foot landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after Lugar left the office with the keys to your jeep?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: After a certain time, he probably found the garage and the jeep, and he came back in it. He returned upstairs, where we were. Then he sat at a desk where there was a telephone. He dialed a number. And I concluded from the conversation he had that he was talking to his wife or maybe his girlfriend. He mentioned Kragujevac. And then he said, "Listen to how these balijas are crying and this president we have caught." He was referring to Tihic. And the telephone was connected to the receiver, so he carried all this closer to Tihic, beating him on the head with his truncheon. And of course, he screamed in pain. And he put the receiver next to one of us and then another one. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: this lasted perhaps some 20 minutes or half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and your brother beaten during that episode?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Lugar beat us together with them, and he also put the receiver close to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said sometime during the evening, about 10.00 p.m., you left that room.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: The five of us were taken downstairs. We were directed, together with a few other people who came out of other rooms, toward the big iron gate of the Territorial Defence. And as we were crossing over to there with our hands on our heads, soldiers were standing on either side of us, and these policemen hurrying along, hitting us with various objects, that is, the weapons they were wielding.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say anything as they struck you with a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. They kept cursing us. Some of them cursed our balija mothers, others cursed our Ustasha mothers. I think they were referring to those of us who were Croats. And when they cursed our balija mothers, they were referring to those of us who were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you eventually enter the gate into the TO courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, I received a severe blow to the back which propelled me through the gate, and there somebody helped me. Because I stumbled, so someone helped me to straighten myself up. And we were put into a room which was five by five metres, and there we found about 30 more people who had also been beaten. They were all townspeople from our town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me step back for one second. You indicated you were hit in the back. Do you know what you were hit with? Was it a fist or an object of some kind?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: It was a military rifle, or rather, it was the rifle butt of a military rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They place you in this room, five by five metres, you said. How many other people were in this room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I have already said that we found about 30 people who had been beaten like us, who were covered in blood, as we were. They had swollen faces, just as we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnic composition of the persons in that room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I think that there were as many Croats as there were Muslims, and there were even a few regular policemen who worked in the police station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the condition of those police officers that were in that room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They had also been beaten up. They had big swellings on their faces. They were covered with blood, just as we were. Their uniforms were stained with blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of these individuals in the military or wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The prisoners, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: No, none of them was wearing a military uniform, but as I have already said, there were a few regular police officers who had been employed in the police station, and a few of them were wearing police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any of the people who were prisoners at the time, were any of these people Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Not for the first few days. Afterwards, they brought in Dragan Mirin, as we used to call him. I think his father was a Serb and his mother a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people standing or sitting on the floor?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We were sitting on the floor. Those other people were sitting on the floor too. That's how I found them, leaning against three walls of that small room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of floor -- flooring was there? Was it wood? Were there mats on there? Was it rugged? Was it -- what was it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Just concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness last prepared a diagram. I have served the diagram upon counsel. There is one which is in Bosnian Croatian and there is another which is Bosnian Croatian with the English subtitles so we know what the words mean. I'd like to place the diagram on the ELMO and leave it there, and at different times during his testimony about the TO he can refer to it, some of the beatings, where they occurred, in the courtyard, where inside the building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I've given those to the registrar already. If the usher could place one on the ELMO. First, could we start off at the bottom just for one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, can you show us where the police station is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, sir, just one step back. Did you prepare this?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A few days ago? A few days ago, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: A few days ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, could you show us where the TO is?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you, going around to the left, tell us what these different structures are in the area? Starting with the TO or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: This is the TO building. In the corner of that building was a toilet, and we all used that toilet if we were allowed to do so. Next to the building is the garage. Then this was an iron gate. These are the warehouses or storerooms. This is the room in which we were incarcerated. There were between 40 and 50 of us in this small space. We were lined up from the entrance door here right round the walls of the room. That's how we sat, on the concrete floor, leaning against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is this building or this room in front of the detention room?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: It was a shop selling spare parts for cars. It is within this complex, but actually, it was separate. It was a separate car spare parts shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If we could leave the ELMO on and he can refer to it, with the Court's permission, later in his testimony, so the usher doesn't have to go back and forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We could leave the ELMO on, and that way the usher doesn't have to go back and forth, and he can refer to it during his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you wish to have these diagrams produced into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have that marked?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence to the diagram? No. Can we have the numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P29 ter and P29, the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever heard of a person named Laki?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was another special forces person from Serbia who, on that evening when they transferred us to the room where we were all incarcerated in, he arrived with another man of the special forces also from Serbia. And I saw around his neck, on the neck of this second special forces person whom they called Kralj [sic] or "King," my gold chain with the locket on which my nickname had been engraved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the same gold chain that just a few hours before Lugar had stolen from you or had robbed from you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the chain that Lugar seized from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Laki and -- do you know the full name of that gentleman who you referred to as the King? Is that Goran Simic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say now whether it was Goran Simic or not, but Kralj [sic] -- I think Kralj [sic] was Goran Simic, but I'm not quite sure because a lot of time has gone by, so I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When those two soldiers entered the room, what did they make you do? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They made us sing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to assist my learned colleague from Prosecution, the nickname of this Goran Simic, probably was not Kralj [sic] like "King." The witness said "Tralja." "T" like Tango, Romeo, et cetera. So I mean, we are going, you know, in new questions, and then the same nickname is used, which is not "King." Actually, it was Tralja, T-r-a-l-j-a, as the witness said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the nickname of the second person who was wearing your stolen gold chain Tralja?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I think it was Tralja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that they asked you to sing Chetnik songs. Who asked you to sing Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: That was Laki and the one with my chain around his neck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once you started singing those Chetnik or Serbian patriotic songs, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Two of them came up to me and my brother. Laki made me - and he beat me on the head while he was doing this, and because my brother and I were sitting next to each other, and he was beating with a police truncheon on my head - he made me laugh. He ordered me to laugh. And then he moved towards my brother and started beating him, and he kept ordering me to keep on laughing. And then he swore at me and cursed my mother because I was laughing while he was beating my brother, saying, "See what your brother is like. Fuck him. He's laughing while we're beating you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he beating you and your brother with?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: A police truncheon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that beating last?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps 10 to 15 minutes, and then he would move on to other people. They would move on to others, whom they then started beating. And this went on for about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how long were you held at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They kept us there for about eight to ten days. I can't remember exactly. But some came a day earlier. We came on the 18th, in the evening; that is to say, we were transferred there then. So some people might have been there nine days, eight days, others ten days. I'm not quite sure. Afterwards they would bring in more people, who spent a shorter period of time there. For example, two or three -- for two or three days they kept bringing new people in and throwing them into our room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time you were at the Territorial Defence, were any of the prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They beat everybody mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were prisoners beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Several times a day, and several times during the night too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did this happen every day that you were there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the people beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They beat them wherever they could. There were no special parts of the body. All over the body, including the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the building? Were they beaten in the courtyard? Were they beaten in the TO building? Were they beaten in the detention room? In what location were the people beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They beat them in the room we were in. They also beat them outside, in the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often were they beaten in the yard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Mostly in the yard when the small group of people came to beat the prisoners. Then what happened was that they would take two of us out at a time, two or three out at a time, and then three or four of them would attack us, beating us with their rifles, kicking us with their army boots, police truncheons. Then they would send us back and the other people had to stand up and sing Chetnik songs as loud as possible. We would go back, and they would take three other people out. And this went on for as long as an hour sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How severe were the beatings in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: So severe that we could barely make it back to the room on our own, it was so painful. We were barely able to walk, so sometimes we'd crawl back into the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the victims of these beatings, did they ever cry out or make any sounds during the beatings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. The people would scream out in pain and beg them to stop, asking why they were being beaten, but they were cries and screams more than ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the soldiers, did they say anything during these beatings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They would usually swear, using different swear words, but usually they would swear -- curse our balija mothers or our Ustasha mothers. They would beat us as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the tone of their voice as they swore at you or cursed you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They tried to speak as loudly as possible, to swear and curse as loudly as possible and to instil even greater fear in us, in those of us who had to take all those beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did a beating session last in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that they lasted up to an hour, until we all took turns, all those who were imprisoned in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... particular session for the two or three people who were brought out, was there any regular time or general time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: No, there was no regular time or general time. Some people were beaten more, others less. But generally speaking, for them to beat us all lasted about an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did they use any implements when they beat you? Please tell the Chamber what type of instruments were used during these beatings.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: They beat us with different implements. In the garage which was adjoined to the TO building itself, there was an old truck, army truck, belonging to the JNA, where there were various wooden and metal objects. So they beat us with that and also with the weapons they had with them, and if anybody had a police truncheon, they would use that. Also, if some of us fell down, then they would usually be kicked with an army boot in the body or neck or head. So they used everything they had to hand to inflict as much pain as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, as a few prisoners are being beaten in the courtyard, what would the rest of the prisoners be doing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: The rest of the prisoners had to stand up against the wall and sing Chetnik songs which they were ordered to sing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the names of any of these Chetnik songs or Serbian patriotic songs, Mr. Bicic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the beginning, the most frequent one was, until we had all learnt the words, the lyrics, "from Topala to Ravna Gora." That was one of them. And later on, somebody who had been taught to sing some of these songs before, they were made to sing songs with similar lyrics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: We sang, as I say, "from Topala to Ravna Gora," and "General Draza's guards are standing all around." General Draza Mihajlovic was a Chetnik in World War II. He was proclaimed a war criminal. Then they made us sing "King Petar send a salad. They will be meat. We'll slaughter Croats to go with it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Then we had to sing "Oy, balija, we're going to slit your throats in this war like Milos did for Murat." And we had to sing in a circle one song after another while they were taking people out to beat them in the yard of the Territorial Defence building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with a soldier by the name of Cera?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where he's from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: He is from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Cera at the TO?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was always with a large group of people from Serbia, the ones who came to beat us. He was one of their informers, and he would point a finger or a police baton that he always had with him. He would point to individuals, who would then be taken out and beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you said, Cera was a local person. He wasn't from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: He was from Samac. I saw him before and I knew him. He's quite a bit younger than me, but I knew him because he often helped or worked in the bakery, the bakery that we -- which supplied us with our bread before we opened the pizzeria. This bakery supplied us with buns, and we would serve Bosnian specialties such as Cevapcici in those buns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw Cera at the TO, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: He was also wearing a camouflage uniform, and he wore dark glasses. He always had a police baton in his right hand and a rifle in his left, so that he would point with that baton and beat the prisoners with it too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recall an incident which occurred between Cera and Omer Nalic between April 22nd and 24th, 1992? At the TO, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Tribunal what happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: On that day, Cera came in with some other men who were also wearing uniforms. They made us get up and sing the Chetnik songs once again. He would beat people with his baton, the ones he selected, and that's how he hit Omer Nalic on one occasion. Nalic asked why, and then he took out a bayonet from his belt, pulled out a bayonet and stuck the knife in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when this occurred and Omer Nalic was stabbed with a bayonet?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: I was a few metres away from Omer. We were standing opposite to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after he was stabbed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: After a few minutes had gone by, he took out my brother and me, [redacted] Dragan Lukac, Izet Izetbegovic. That's what they did. They would always take us out, almost always. Sometimes two by two, three by three, and then four people or five people, depending on how many soldiers there were from Serbia in the yard and in the room itself where we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened in the yard? Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: In the yard, there were about 30 to 40 soldiers. So they took us out, four or five of us, and they distributed us around the yard. I can indicate this on the map --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: -- on the diagram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One second. Let us go to the video. Please show us.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: It was here by the water pump. It was a hand water pump --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: -- or tap. And they beat me. That's where I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED BICIC
utterances.text: In this corner here, Cera stopped beating me and some others and then he proceeded to beat my brother. And when they knocked him down to the ground, when he fell down from the blows, Cera, with his boot, kicked him in his open hand breaking three of his fingers. In this area here towards the garage and iron gate, they beat Dragan Lukac. They were beating Dragan Lukac at that time. And when they had had their fill, they would make us get back into the room, beating us all the time on our backs. And then they would take other people out, and they would beat them in similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, should we break here or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's 1700 hours. We shall break, and we shall continue tomorrow morning at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
